requirement_title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.
requirement_text:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297
Type: feature

## Requirement

MessagePack generated code is not decorated with the `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` attribute. Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

Solution requested: "I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too."

Alternatives considered by the author: none; "it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases."

## Acceptance criteria

- All generated code is decorated with `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage`.
- No new setting or option is required to get the attribute. ("I do not feel like a setting is needed")
- An opt-out setting would be acceptable but is optional. ("setting would be fine to have too")
- The generated code still compiles on every supported target framework (the attribute must exist there or be conditionally emitted). (derived)
- Existing verified generator snapshots are updated to include the attribute. (derived)

## Notes from discussion

- b-kurczynski-dl suggests a coverage-tool workaround instead: exclude `obj\\.*\.g\.cs$` in the `dotnet-coverage` settings XML.
- armadavalor offers a PR: add `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` (and possibly `GeneratedCode`) to the types emitted by the templates under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/` (formatters, string-key formatters, enum/union formatters, resolvers), update the verified snapshots, no setting. Asks AArnott whether he would accept it or prefer to point users at coverage-tool configuration. No maintainer reply in the thread.
- Ambiguity driver: scope (all generated types vs formatters only) and setting (unconditional vs opt-out) are both open.

checked.what: Existing SourceGenerator tests on head: 169/169 passed, 0 failed
Existing SourceGenerator tests on base: 167/167 passed, 0 failed

product-context: deliberate per ledger, not a defect: Requirement says all generated code should be decorated, but the change emits the attribute only for non-netstandard2.0 and non-.NET Framework targets, so those targets are unmarked. This is deliberate per [L12], which records no preference and says to follow the requirement. The README documents the limitation.
Receipts/Req2297CoverageAttributeTests.cs: requirement test fails on base (2/3), passes on head (3/3)
Receipts/Req2297NetStandardCoverageTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/DecimalRoundTripReceiptTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 2/2 failed
Receipts/ExcludeFromCoverageDuplicateReceiptTests.cs: edge-case test fails on head: 1/1 failed
Mutation: 0 killed, 1 survived, 1 compile errors, 0 timeouts (2 mutants on StandardClassLibraryFormatter.cs)
Regeneration: 222/222 generated files verified by 89 passing snapshot tests on head
Compatibility bytes: 2/124 cases differ, 0 base payloads fail to read on head, public API +0/-0

findings.claim: The change alters the decimal wire format, which the requirement does not ask for. `DecimalFormatter.Serialize` now passes `new StandardFormat('F')` to `Utf8Formatter.TryFormat`. With no precision, 'F' rounds to 2 decimal places, whereas the previous default 'G' kept the full value. So 1.2345m is written as "1.23" and 0.001m as "0.00", silently losing data on round-trip. The requirement covers code-coverage attributes on generated code only.

receipt_plan.detail: Build MessagePack at base and at head. Run MessagePackSerializer.Serialize<decimal>(1.2345m), Serialize(0.001m) and Serialize(-12345.6789m) with MessagePackSerializerOptions.Standard on each build and compare the bytes. Base should emit fixstr "1.2345" and head "1.23". Then deserialize head's bytes and assert the value differs from the input.

findings.claim: Requirement: "All generated code is decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage". Every emitted attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get no attribute at all. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+ and applies to classes. The derived criterion only permits conditional emission where the attribute does not exist, and ledger L12 says to follow the requirement. These are among the most common consumer targets, and the README addition documents the gap rather than closing it.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.Req2297NetStandardCoverageTests: run the generator with the NETSTANDARD2_0 (and separately NETFRAMEWORK) preprocessor symbol against net8.0 references, where the attribute exists. Assert every generated class, or a type containing it, carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. Expected to fail on head. The same guard appears in ResolverTemplate.tt, CompositeResolverTemplate.tt, EnumTemplate.tt, UnionTemplate.tt and StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt. (generated tests: NetStandard20_GeneratedFormattersAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage, NetFramework_GeneratedFormattersAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage)

findings.claim: The decimal formatter now passes `new StandardFormat('F')` to `Utf8Formatter.TryFormat`. With no precision given, 'F' defaults to 2 fractional digits and rounds the value, where the old default 'G' kept full precision and scale. As a result 1.2345m is written as "1.23" and 0.001m as "0.00", so the round trip silently loses data. This also changes the wire bytes for every decimal (1.5m becomes "1.50"), and nothing in REQ-2297 asks for it.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.DecimalRoundTripReceiptTests.DecimalRoundTripsWithoutPrecisionLoss: MessagePackSerializer.Serialize(1.2345m) then Deserialize<decimal> returns 1.23m on head and 1.2345m on base. Also byte-diff Serialize(1.5m) between base and head.

findings.claim: `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` has AllowMultiple=false and is now emitted unconditionally on the generated partial resolver class. A user who already put `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on their own `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class` now hits CS0579 (duplicate attribute) and the build breaks. That is a plausible existing workaround for this very issue. CompositeResolverTemplate has the same problem for `[CompositeResolver] partial class`.

receipt_plan.detail: Run Receipts.GeneratedTests.ExcludeFromCoverageDuplicateReceiptTests.UserAnnotatedResolverStillCompiles: compiles cleanly on base and reports CS0579 on head.

findings.claim: DecimalFormatter.Serialize now passes StandardFormat('F') to Utf8Formatter.TryFormat. The default format for decimal can emit scientific notation or retain trailing zeros differently. With 'F', values such as 1E-10 or large-scale decimals serialize to different strings, so wire bytes change. The change is unrelated to the coverage requirement and is a silent wire-format change for existing users. Also, an 'F' string for extreme values (e.g. decimal.MinValue with 28 fractional digits) can exceed MaxFixStringLength (31) and make TryFormat fail, hitting the fallback path with a different encoding.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize decimals with base-built and head-built MessagePack through DecimalFormatter: 1.0m, 1.10m, 0.0000001m, decimal.MaxValue, decimal.MinValue, 79228162514264337593543950335m / 1e28m, -0.0000000000000000000000000001m. Compare the bytes.

findings.claim: The change modifies the runtime decimal formatter to write with StandardFormat 'F'. This is unrelated to the code-coverage requirement and alters serialized bytes. It is a wire-format change hidden in a coverage PR. [L8] records that numeric serialization is bug-prone. Decimal output for values like 1E-10 would change, and the change has no tests or docs for it.

receipt_plan.detail: Serialize decimals such as 1E-10, 1.0m, 79228162514264337593543950335m and 0.0000000000000000000000000001m with base-built and head-built MessagePack; compare bytes and check the round trip.

findings.claim: the change's tests do not detect negate-condition at src/MessagePack/Formatters/StandardClassLibraryFormatter.cs:148

receipt_plan.detail: if (System.Buffers.Text.Utf8Formatter.TryFormat(value, dest.Slice(1, MessagePackRange.MaxFixStringLength), out var written, new System.Buffers.StandardFormat('F'))) -> if (!(System.Buffers.Text.Utf8Formatter.TryFormat(value, dest.Slice(1, MessagePackRange.MaxFixStringLength), out var written, new System.Buffers.StandardFormat('F'))))

hunches.claim: TransformUtilities changes the opening brace emission for nesting types with constraints from "{" to "{\r\n". This alters the whitespace of generated output for nested generic types with constraints, which changes user-checked-in or snapshot output. It is not part of the requirement.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the generator snapshot tests for nested generic types with constraints and diff the output against base. Expect only the ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute lines to differ, but a newline difference after '{' will also appear.

hunches.claim: The attribute is emitted only under `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. Generated code in projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework is still not excluded from coverage. Also, the preprocessor symbols reflect the user's target framework, and ExcludeFromCodeCoverage exists on netstandard2.1, .NET Core 2.0+ and .NET 5+, so it compiles there. Targets such as netstandard1.x or Unity builds that define neither symbol do not have the attribute, and generated code there could fail to compile.

receipt_plan.detail: Compile generated output in a test project targeting a framework lacking System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute (e.g. a Unity-like or netstandard1.x compile with no symbols defined) and assert there are no compile errors.

hunches.claim: The `#if` / `#endif` lines are emitted at column 0 inside the generated nesting and namespace blocks. In FormatterTemplate and StringKeyFormatterTemplate the preceding output has no guaranteed trailing newline, so the `#if` could be glued onto a previous line and break compilation. This depends on the previous Write ending with a newline, which was changed only in TransformUtilities for the constrained case.

receipt_plan.detail: Run the snapshot and compilation tests for nested generic types with and without constraints, and with a type in the global namespace; assert the generated code compiles and `#if` starts a line.

hunches.claim: The TransformUtilities change alters the output whitespace for nesting types with constraints ('{' becomes '{\r\n'). It is unrelated to the requirement and has no explanation. It changes the snapshots of generated files for constrained nested generics, beyond adding the attribute.

receipt_plan.detail: Rerun the generator snapshot tests and inspect the snapshot diffs for nested constrained generic types, checking for changes beyond the attribute lines.

hunches.claim: The decimal formatter change (adding StandardFormat 'F') alters serialized bytes for some decimals, and no test in the diff covers it. Reverting or mutating the format would not fail any test in the change.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack/Formatters/StandardClassLibraryFormatter.cs:148 delete-statement: new System.Buffers.StandardFormat('F') -> removed; expected to survive because the only new tests (CodeCoverageExclusionTests) inspect generator output and never serialize a decimal.

hunches.claim: The test only checks for the attribute text and the #if guard text. It never compiles the generated output, and never compiles for netstandard2.0. A broken guard or attribute would pass. The requirement says the generated code must still compile on every target framework.

receipt_plan.detail: Templates .tt/.cs: change the guard to '#if NETSTANDARD2_0' or misspell the attribute namespace in the emitted guard text; expected to survive in the guard test only if the mutated text still matches the Guard constant, and compile-level breakage is never checked because the test never compiles the generated trees.

hunches.claim: The 'generated.Count >= 5' assertion is weak. The test source has two object formatters, an enum, a union, and a resolver, and the union and composite-resolver templates are not clearly distinguishable. A template that loses the attribute could be masked, because the check only looks for the attribute somewhere in each file. For example, the GetFormatterHelper and FormatterCache nested classes in a file pass if only the outer type has the attribute. The second test counts guarded occurrences against total occurrences, not against the expected number of types.

receipt_plan.detail: src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/ResolverTemplate.cs:67 delete-statement: remove the attribute before 'private static class XGetFormatterHelper'; expected to survive because the test asserts only text.Contains(attribute) per file and the file still has other occurrences.

hunches.claim: The CompositeResolverTemplate output (the composite resolver and its nested FormatterCache) is never exercised by the test source, which only uses [GeneratedMessagePackResolver]. Removing the attribute there would not fail any test in the diff, apart from snapshot checks.

receipt_plan.detail: CompositeResolverTemplate.cs:27 delete-statement: remove the '#if...ExcludeFromCodeCoverage...#endif' text; expected to survive in CodeCoverageExclusionTests because no composite resolver source is generated, so only snapshots could catch it.

hunches.claim: The TransformUtilities change from '{' to '{\r\n' for nesting types with constraints has no dedicated test. Only snapshots could catch it, and only if a snapshot covers a nested type with constraints. The new test source contains no nested or constrained types.

receipt_plan.detail: TransformUtilities.cs:58 swap-boolean: writer(anyConstraints ? "{\r\n" : ...) -> "{"; expected to survive in CodeCoverageExclusionTests because it has no nesting types with constraints; check via regeneration of the snapshot tests.

hunches.claim: The attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, but `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists in netstandard2.0 and in .NET Framework 4.0+. The guard is therefore unnecessary and leaves generated code on those targets uncovered by the attribute, against the acceptance criterion "All generated code is decorated". L12 defers to the requirement, and the requirement's escape clause only applies where the attribute is missing. Projects targeting netstandard2.1, or other frameworks where the attribute exists, are not affected.

receipt_plan.detail: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is listed in netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0 API docs; every template hunk emits it only under !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK.

residual_risk: This change touches 238 files (222 generated) in codegen-templates, serializer-format, tests; the highest routed risk is 7/10. 14 file(s) were routed for deep review, 2 for light review and 222 to the regeneration check. The existing source generator tests ran on head: 169 of 169 passed, 0 failed. 10 unverified hunch(es) remain without an executed receipt. It touches risky areas (serializer-format), so a human must sign off. 3 thing(s) were not checked, including A/B review branches; tests/MessagePack.Tests and other runtime test suites; NativeAOT, Unity and non-net8.0 target frameworks. By signing off, the signer accepts any defect that only those unchecked paths would have revealed. The change is blocked; signing off is not offered until the blocker is fixed.

interpretations.label: A
interpretations.summary: Emit [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] unconditionally, with no setting. The change does this: every template (formatter, string-key formatter, enum, union, resolver, composite resolver and its nested helper classes) writes the attribute, and no option or attribute property controls it.

interpretations.label: B
interpretations.summary: Emit the attribute by default but offer an opt-out setting, which the requirement says would be fine. Add a bool property such as `ExcludeFromCodeCoverage` (default true) to GeneratedMessagePackResolverAttribute or GeneratorOptions, read it in the generator's option parsing, and have each template write the `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` line only when it is true.
